title: Violin Concerto in D major
hook: It begins with five soft drumbeats, and the violin sings rather than shows off.

painting.title: Marie Joséphine Charlotte du Val d’Ognes (Young Woman Drawing)
painting.collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
painting.pairingNote: A young woman drawing by a bright window in Paris in 1801; stillness, concentration and clear light, like the violin’s long singing line.

facts: Beethoven wrote the concerto in 1806 for Franz Clement, one of the leading violinists in Vienna, and Clement gave the premiere on 23 December 1806 at the Theater an der Wien. Beethoven is believed to have finished the solo part so late that Clement had to play some of it at sight.

The premiere was not a success, and the concerto was rarely played for almost forty years. In 1844, twelve-year-old Joseph Joachim played it in London with Felix Mendelssohn conducting, and from then on it became one of the central works for the violin.
Instead of fireworks, the soloist mostly sings: long, high melodies and decorations above the orchestra. The opening five drumbeats return throughout the first movement.

Beethoven also arranged the concerto for piano and orchestra. For that version he wrote a long first-movement [[cadenza|cadenza]] in which the timpani join the soloist; this recording uses it, adapted for the violin.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a broad, serene first movement held together by a drumbeat (I), a hushed set of variations (II), a hunting-song rondo that follows without a break (III).

movements.heading: Allegro ma non troppo
movements.summary: Five soft strokes on the timpani, then a calm tune in the woodwinds. The orchestra presents all the themes first; only after three and a half minutes does the violin enter, climbing from low to very high, and go through them again in its own way. That is the Classical [[double-exposition|double exposition]]. The movement is long and unhurried, and the drumbeat keeps coming back underneath.

mainIdeas.name: The drumbeat
mainIdeas.description: five even, quiet strokes, first on the timpani, later in the strings, winds and brass.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a calm, gentle tune in the woodwinds.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a melody that rises and falls in scales, first in the major, then in the minor.

stops.happening: The opening. The drumbeat becomes the movement’s pulse

stops.happening: A first shadow (a D-sharp, outside the key)

stops.hear: Clarinets and bassoons sing a new melody in scales; then it turns to the minor

High above the orchestra, the violin sings the opening tune
The violin holds a long, shimmering [[trill|trill]] while the woodwinds play Theme 2 below it

Very quiet and sad: the violin sings a slow melody in G minor; the drumbeat continues softly below
stops.happening: The darkest, stillest passage of the movement

stops.hear: The opening theme in the full orchestra, loud and grand
The violin plays alone; partway through, the timpani join in, beating the opening rhythm under the violin

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The violin, low and very quiet, plays Theme 2; then the orchestra ends with firm chords

notice: Count how many times you hear the drumbeat of five even notes. It moves from the timpani to the strings, the woodwinds and the trumpets.
In the cadenza, listen for the timpani. A cadenza is usually for the soloist alone; here the drum joins in.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Schneiderhan plays Beethoven’s own cadenzas, taken from the piano version of the concerto and adapted for the violin by Schneiderhan himself. Many violinists play Fritz Kreisler’s cadenzas instead. On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 1–3, followed by Mozart’s Violin Concerto No. 5.

movements.heading: Larghetto
movements.summary: A slow, hushed movement in G major. The muted strings play a simple theme; then horn, clarinet and bassoon take it in turn while the violin weaves fine decorations above them. The violin sings a new melody of its own, the theme returns, and an orchestral outburst leads to a short solo that runs straight into the finale.

mainIdeas.name: The theme
mainIdeas.description: a slow, simple melody for [[muted|muted]] strings.

mainIdeas.name: The violin’s song
mainIdeas.description: a tender melody of its own, heard twice.

stops.hear: Muted strings play a slow, hushed theme
stops.happening: The theme, in G major. The movement is a set of quiet [[variation|variation]]s on it

stops.hear: The solo violin enters, weaving fine decorations high above while the horn, then the clarinet, carry the theme
stops.happening: The violin decorates rather than leads

stops.hear: The violin sings a new melody of its own, simple and tender
stops.happening: A second theme, for the soloist

stops.hear: The theme returns quietly in the strings, with the violin floating above

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: A sudden loud outburst from the orchestra; then the violin alone plays a short, free passage
stops.happening: A brief [[cadenza|cadenza]] that leads straight into the finale ([[attacca|attacca]])

notice: For most of the movement the violin does not play the theme at all. It decorates it, high above, while the orchestra’s instruments take turns with the melody.

movements.heading: Rondo: Allegro
movements.summary: A [[rondo|rondo]] with a hunting-song theme in six beats, first played low on the violin and then shouted back by the whole orchestra. Between its returns come a bright episode and a sadder one in G minor. After the cadenza the theme surfaces in a surprising key before the concerto ends in high spirits.

mainIdeas.name: The rondo theme
mainIdeas.description: a jaunty hunting tune, played first low on the violin.

mainIdeas.name: The G minor episode
mainIdeas.description: a slower-feeling, sad melody shared by the violin and the bassoon.

Rapid runs in the violin and a bright new tune; horns sound hunting calls
The hunting tune returns
A gentler, sadder tune in G minor, sung by the violin and then the bassoon
The hunting tune again
The violin plays alone
The violin plays the tune quietly in an unexpected key; the oboe answers

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A last, quiet echo of the tune, then two loud chords

notice: Listen to the G minor episode. It is the only time the finale looks back to the stillness of the slow movement.

threads.title: The drumbeat
threads.body: Five even notes open the concerto, return all through the first movement and come back in the timpani during Beethoven’s cadenza.

threads.title: Song, not show
threads.body: The violin spends most of the concerto singing and decorating, high above the orchestra, rather than competing with it.

threads.title: Linked movements
threads.body: The slow movement does not end: a short solo carries it straight into the finale.
